notes: B3 · SEPTEMBER STRUCTURES. Endless mode milestones, one every 8 endless weeks, so long runs have chapters instead of pure ratchet. Fired as a modal + log entry; {agent} substitutes the run's most-dispatched agent. Cycles after the last. Expanded 6->12 (2026-08-19): the pool cycles (due-1)%size, so six entries repeated verbatim from endless week 56; twelve pushes first verbatim repeat past week 100.

milestones.title: A LETTER, FORWARDED TWICE
milestones.body:
It reaches the board with two forwarding stamps and a coffee ring that is not yours. {agent}'s hand.

'I hear the board is still up. Of course it is. You should know the thing nobody tells you at the start: it does not end because the problems end. It ends when you can hand it to somebody and sleep. I could not, for the longest time, and then one Tuesday I could.

Don't write back. Resolve something with the time instead. That was always the correspondence.'

No return address. The postmark is a county you've been to.

milestones.title: THE COUNTY MAP, REDRAWN
milestones.body:
The county issues its decennial map revision, off schedule, quietly. You get a copy because Ruth gets everything.

The changes are small and enormous: the timber yard road is a named road now. The estate's retention pond is marked POND (SEASONAL), which is a demotion it earned. And the stretch of river country the board has defended all this time is labeled, for the first time in county history, in the smallest approved font, with its own name instead of 'unincorporated.'

Nobody petitioned for that. Somebody in the map office just knew. That is what winning looks like at cartographic speed.

milestones.title: THE LEDGER, ANNOTATED
milestones.body:
The fifth fingerprint's photograph of the ledger page — the one filed under the floorboard of the mind — has changed, which photographs do not do.

In the margin, in the hand that predates ruling, a new note against the summer's column of adjustments and absorptions:

'STILL OPERATING. NOTED WITHOUT PREJUDICE. THE OVERHEAD REMAINS ACCEPTABLE — TO BOTH LEDGERS.'

It is the closest thing to professional respect the tower has ever extended. The board decides, unanimously, without discussing it, never to mention it again.

milestones.title: THE FIRST WINTER GENERAL MEETING
milestones.body:
The co-op was a summer thing. Everyone knew that the way everyone knows a creek is seasonal.

Tonight the diner stays open late for the first WINTER general meeting — coats on the backs of chairs, the good coffee urn, agenda items that assume a future ('spring courier routes,' 'the estate seed library'). Attendance: everyone. Including three people nobody recruited who heard there was a thing you could join that fixed what the county wouldn't.

The minutes are two pages. The precedent is permanent. You are no longer running a response. You are running an institution, and institutions get to outlive their emergencies.

milestones.title: THE SECOND SPRING
milestones.body:
The board has now operated longer past the summer than the summer itself lasted.

Somewhere in the file a founding purpose is written down, and the board has quietly outgrown it the way a windbreak outgrows the field plan — still doing the job, also now HABITAT. Problems arrive and are handled by people who learned from people you dispatched. Two of the demons have started describing their arrangements as 'standing.' The tower watches an operation that no longer needs watching to keep operating.

There is no mechanical reward for this. There is just the fact of it, which you built, one Sunday at a time.

milestones.title: THE RELAY
milestones.body:
A letter arrives addressed not to the board but to 'WHOEVER KEEPS THE BOARD NOW' — from a town two counties over, describing their own summer: their own estate, their own timber yard, their own tower they are not sure they are allowed to mention.

'We heard how you organized. We copied the parts we understood. What did we miss?'

Ruth drafts the reply the way she does everything: completely. The package goes out Tuesday — templates, phone-tree diagrams, the courier math, and one sentence of cover letter: 'You missed nothing. It is exactly as much work as it looks like. Start anyway.'

The board is a seed now. Endless was the point.

milestones.title: SOMEBODY ASKS TO LEARN THE BOARD
milestones.body:
A kid from the Estates — one of the ones who grew up on the other side of the problems you routed — asks, through {agent}, whether the board takes an apprentice.

You say what Pop said, because it is the only thing there is to say: 'It takes a person who keeps showing up. Come Sunday.'

They come Sunday. They are terrible at it. They come the Sunday after that, which is the whole qualification.

milestones.title: THE MODEM IS REPLACED (THE OLD ONE STAYS)
milestones.body:
The modem finally dies on a Tuesday, mid-handshake, after decades of duty. {agent} drives the replacement down from the county seat the same afternoon, which tells you what the network has become to everyone who says they only check it sometimes.

The old modem does not leave the shelf. It sits beside its successor like a retired dog next to the working one. Nobody suggests otherwise.

milestones.title: A LEDGER AUDIT, VOLUNTARY
milestones.body:
You go back through the whole ledger one evening, every line since Memorial Day of the first summer. {agent} sits across the desk and reads the lines you slide over.

The finding of the audit is this: the handwriting changes in the hard weeks. It presses deeper. You can date every crisis in the county by the depth of the pencil.

You file the audit under: known.

milestones.title: THE COUNTY OFFERS TO MAKE IT OFFICIAL
milestones.body:
A letter on county letterhead proposes to recognize 'the coordination network' as a volunteer emergency-preparedness entity, with a small stipend and a reporting requirement.

You read it twice. {agent} reads it once and laughs at the same sentence both of you knew was the problem: REPORTING REQUIREMENT.

The reply is polite and handwritten and declines. Some things work because nobody has to certify that they do.

milestones.title: THE QUESTION, ASKED OUT LOUD AGAIN
milestones.body:
It has been long enough that the W11 question — the one that took fifteen years to ask the first time — is due again, and this time it is {agent} who asks it, over the desk, not unkindly:

'Who takes the board after you?'

You look at the roster. The roster looks back. It is a better answer than it was the first time somebody asked, and you say so, and that is as far as the evening gets. Far enough.

milestones.title: THE QUIETEST STRETCH THE LEDGER HAS EVER HELD
milestones.body:
You notice it only because the ledger measures it: the longest run of ordinary weeks since the board began. No spikes. No burns. The gumbo accounted for.

{agent} says the dangerous thing out loud: 'Maybe it's done.'

The board is not done — the board is a river, and this is a wide slow reach of it. But you let the sentence sit on the desk a full minute before you file it, because it earned the minute.

apprentice.comment: ENDLESS V2 · THE APPRENTICE. m7/m11 narrated succession; this mechanizes it. Aria is the canon candidate — the summer vignette where Nicola brings her to the office and she asks what the modem sounds like when it dials is the foreshadow.
apprentice.offer_title: SOMEBODY AT THE DOOR ON A SUNDAY
apprentice.offer_body:
Aria is at the office door at seven — Nicola's kid, the one who asked what the dial-up sounds like and then nodded once, like the sound had settled something.

She does not ask to watch. She asks for the board's smallest problem and a pencil.

Pop's rule sits on the desk between you: it takes a person who keeps showing up. She has been showing up for weeks. You just hadn't written it down yet.
apprentice.accept_line: Aria takes the corner of the desk that catches the lamp. The ledger gains a second handwriting, small and very careful.
apprentice.decline_line: She nods like a person filing a decision rather than accepting one, and leaves. The knock will come again. Some questions keep Sunday hours.
training_lines: Aria spends Sunday tracing last month's dispatches backwards, asking why at every junction. Twice you don't have an answer, and she writes THAT down.
Aria alphabetizes the stamp drawer. It was alphabetized. Now it is more so. The board tolerates the audit.
Aria reads the region files cover to cover with her feet hooked on the chair rung. At the Graustark file she goes quiet for a long time and does not ask anything at all.
Aria drills the dial-up handshake until she can hum it. She says every machine says its name if you wait for the end of the sentence.
misroute_lines: Aria routes the Verbena Way letters to the wrong week and the problem grows a ring. She finds the error herself, which is the whole lesson, and it costs the board a little to teach it.
Aria dispatches by the map instead of by the people and the map, as usual, lies. You unpick it together on Monday. The ledger notes the tuition.
Aria answers the office line in her own voice. Whoever it was hangs up, and calls back Thursday asking for her.
small_ones_lines: Aria takes the week's smallest problem off the board before you reach the desk. Her resolution note is one sentence. It is the correct sentence.
The little trouble at the edge of the map is gone by Sunday supper. Aria's pencil mark where it stood is so faint you check it twice.
Aria handles the small one the way Pop handled small ones — by making it never have been a problem in anyone's memory but the ledger's.
One of the week's minor aches resolves without a dispatch. In the margin, in the second handwriting: 'talked to them. it was about the fence. it is not about the fence now.'
Aria clears the smallest line item and leaves the pencil exactly where you leave it, which is its own message.
The board's littlest fire goes out quietly midweek. Aria doesn't mention it. The ledger does.
apprentice.graduate_line: Four Sundays in, Aria stops asking why at the junctions. She has started asking why not, which is a different apprenticeship entirely. The small ones are hers now.
apprentice.handoff_header: You set the pencil down. She picks it up before it stops rolling.
handoff_lines: The board does not retire. The board changes hands the way the bowls do — while everyone is looking somewhere else.
Nicola cries once, at the door, and denies it at the bottom of the stairs.
